newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission adopts olive oil reform report.
newsitem.headline: Commission adopts olive oil reform report.

text.p: The European Commission adopted a report on Wednesday suggesting two options for reforming the fraud-ridden olive oil marketing regime, a statement said.

The controversial report has been held up for many months due to opposition from southern producer countries who feared that planned changes would reduce farmers' revenues and lead to a decline in quality.

The first reform option would partially meet criticism from Italian, Spanish, Greek, Portuguese and French producers by maintaining the existing subsidy system -- based on production, consumption, storage and export aids -- while imposing national output limits and reducing intervention storage.

The second and more radical option favoured by the Commission would link subsidies to the number of olive trees and historic yields but allow member states to vary the aid according to environmental, employment and other conditions.

One of the main aims is to simplify the subsidy system to make fraud more difficult. The small producers' aid scheme, which covers around two-thirds of all olive farmers and 20 percent of output, would be scrapped.

With some two million small farmers, the scheme was difficult to control and there was widespread abuse of the system with small producers claiming subsidies twice over and exaggerating tonnages in collusion with the EU's 13,000 mills.
It would be replaced by a single production aid scheme based on oil produced at an approved mill. If production exceeded a national limit then aid would be progressively reduced.
Consumption aid would either be substantially increased to make it effective, or abolished.
Another aim of the reform is to prevent production surpluses following massive new plantings, notably in Spain.

The Commission plans to draft a reform proposal after receiving reactions from producer and trade organisations and the European Parliament and hopes to get agreement from farm ministers in time for the new regime to take effect in the 1998/99 marketing year.
